title: Pillar VI — Git Workflows, Testing & CI/CD

sections.heading: Commits and branches: the mental model
paragraphs: A git commit is a snapshot of the whole project plus a pointer to its parent commit — history is a chain of snapshots, not a pile of diffs. A branch is nothing but a movable label pointing at a commit; creating one is instant and free.

The working cycle: edit files (working directory), `git add` selects changes into the staging area, `git commit` seals the staged snapshot. The staging area exists so you can commit a *coherent subset* of your current mess.
Good commits are atomic — one logical change with a message explaining *why*. 'Fix login redirect for expired sessions' can be reviewed, reverted, and bisected; 'wip stuff' cannot.
sections.summary: A branch is just a lightweight pointer to a commit, so making one is instant and copies nothing.

variants.question: What actually happens when you run `git branch feature-x`?
options: A new label is created that points at the current commit
Every uncommitted change is moved onto the new branch for you
A matching remote branch is created up on the origin server
The whole project is copied into a fresh directory per branch
variants.rationale: Branches are ~40-byte pointers into the commit graph. That's why branching in git is instant and why workflows built on many short-lived branches are practical — there is no duplication to pay for.
optionExplanations: Correct — a branch is a movable pointer, nothing more.
Uncommitted changes belong to the working directory, which is independent of branch pointers (they follow you until committed).
Nothing touches the network until you push — git branch is purely local.
That's how some pre-git systems felt; git branches share the same object store — zero copying.
variants.interviewTip: 'A branch is just a pointer to a commit' is a one-sentence answer that instantly signals you understand git's model rather than memorized commands.

variants.question: You're on `main` with two files edited but not yet committed. You run `git checkout -b hotfix` and then `git commit -am 'patch'`. Where did that new commit land, and what happened to `main`?
options: It landed on `main`, and `hotfix` is an empty copy awaiting its first change
It landed on `hotfix`; `main` still points where it did, one commit behind
Both `main` and `hotfix` advanced, since they started from the same commit
The edits were dropped during checkout, having not been committed first
variants.rationale: `checkout -b hotfix` created a label at the same commit as `main` and moved HEAD onto it, carrying the uncommitted edits along. The commit advances only the branch HEAD points at — `hotfix` — while `main` stays frozen at the older commit. Branches diverge precisely because a commit moves one pointer, not all of them.
optionExplanations: HEAD moved to `hotfix` on creation, so the commit lands there, not on `main` — and it isn't empty, it carried the working-directory edits.
Correct — the commit only advances the branch HEAD is on (`hotfix`); `main` is left one commit behind.
A commit advances a single pointer — the one HEAD references — never two branches at once.
Uncommitted edits follow you across a checkout when there's no conflict; they were never lost.
variants.interviewTip: Say it as 'a commit only moves the branch HEAD is currently on' — that one line explains divergence, fast-forwards, and why other branches don't magically update.

variants.question: `main` and `experiment` both point at commit `abc123`. You run `git branch -d experiment`. What did git actually remove?
options: Commit `abc123` and its snapshot, since a branch owns its own commits
The working-directory files that were created while on `experiment`
Only the `experiment` label — `abc123` stays reachable through `main`
The reflog entries for `experiment`, making the deletion irreversible
variants.rationale: Branches don't own commits — commits live in the shared object store and a branch is merely a ~40-byte pointer into that graph. Deleting `experiment` deletes the pointer and nothing else; since `main` still references `abc123`, the history is untouched. That's why `-d` is instant and why git only warns (`-D`) when deletion would leave commits unreachable.
optionExplanations: No branch owns a commit — commits belong to the object store, and `abc123` is still referenced by `main`.
The working directory is independent of branch pointers; deleting a label never touches your files.
Correct — branch deletion removes a pointer, not history; everything stays reachable via `main`.
Reflogs are per-reference safety nets and the commits persist in the object store — even 'lost' work is typically recoverable.
variants.interviewTip: 'Deleting a branch deletes a pointer, not history' is the mirror image of 'creating a branch copies nothing' — pairing the two shows you truly hold the graph model, not just commands.

variants.question: You run `git switch -c release/v2` from the tip of `main`, then immediately run `git log` on the new branch. It shows the project's entire history. Where is that history stored for `release/v2`?
options: Git copied the commit history into a per-branch log file at creation time
Nowhere new — the ref shares `main`'s commit and `git log` walks its parents
In the staging area, which snapshots full history whenever a branch is made
On the remote — `git log` queries origin to rebuild the new branch's history
variants.rationale: History in git is the chain of parent pointers hanging off whatever commit a ref names. A new branch adds exactly one label; `git log` starts at that commit and follows parents backwards, so the 'branch history' is just the reachable ancestry — shared, not duplicated. This is the structural reason branching is free.
optionExplanations: There is no per-branch history file — history is derived by walking the commit graph, never stored per label.
Correct — one new pointer, zero new data; log is a graph traversal from wherever the ref points.
The staging area holds the next commit's proposed content — it has nothing to do with history or branch creation.
`git log` is fully local; the entire graph already lives in your clone's object store.
variants.interviewTip: If asked 'why is branching cheap in git?', answer structurally: 'a branch is one pointer, and history is just the ancestry walk from it — nothing is copied.' Mechanism beats adjectives.

sections.heading: Merge vs rebase — and the golden rule
paragraphs: `merge` ties two histories together with a merge commit — truthful, but busy repos accumulate a criss-cross graph. `rebase` replays your commits on top of the target branch, yielding a straight line — cleaner, but the replayed commits are *new* commits with new hashes.

That rewrite is why the golden rule exists: never rebase commits that others may have based work on (i.e., anything pushed to a shared branch). Rebase your local feature branch freely; rebase shared history and every collaborator's tree diverges from yours.
A very common team workflow: rebase your feature branch onto main to stay current while developing, then merge (often squash-merge) into main via pull request.
sections.summary: Rebase your own private branches for a tidy history, but never rebase shared history that others build on.

variants.question: A teammate rebased the shared `develop` branch and force-pushed it. Everyone's local `develop` now 'has diverged'. What did the rebase do that caused this?
options: Nothing real — divergence warnings are purely cosmetic and safe to ignore here
It permanently deleted everyone's existing commits from the origin server itself
It rewrote the commits with new hashes, so no clone matches the remote
It merged the `develop` branch into every open feature branch at once
variants.rationale: Rebase creates replacement commits; force-push made the remote point at the rewritten line. Every local clone still holds the old line, so git correctly reports divergence — and anyone who naively merges the two lines resurrects zombie duplicate commits. This is precisely why shared branches are rebase-forbidden.
optionExplanations: Ignoring it and pulling merges the old and new lines together — the graph doubles its commits and the mess compounds.
The old commits still exist in clones and reflogs — the damage is divergence and duplication risk, not immediate deletion.
Correct — rewritten hashes + force-push = every collaborator's history contradicts the remote.
Rebase touches one branch's history; it never fans out into other branches.
variants.interviewTip: When asked merge vs rebase, don't pick a side — state the policy: 'rebase private history for cleanliness, merge shared history for safety, never force-push shared branches.'

variants.question: Your feature branch is 6 commits ahead of `main`, all still local and unpushed. `main` moved ahead with 3 new commits. You want your feature to sit cleanly on top of the latest `main` with no merge commit. Which is safe and appropriate here — and why?
options: Nothing here is safe; any history op on a branch behind `main` risks corrupting the shared repo
`git rebase main`, but only after force-pushing the feature branch first so the remote leads it
`git merge main` into the feature branch, because merging is always the safer default choice here
`git rebase main` on the feature branch — its commits are private, so rewriting hashes is safe
variants.rationale: The golden rule forbids rebasing *shared* history — commits others may have built on. These 6 commits are local and unpushed, so nobody else has them; rewriting their hashes onto the new `main` tip is exactly the sanctioned use of rebase, giving the straight-line history you asked for with zero merge commit.
optionExplanations: The golden rule only restricts *shared* history; local unpushed commits are the textbook case where rebase is encouraged.
Force-pushing before rebasing is backwards and pointless here — the branch is unshared, so there's nothing on the remote to force over.
Merging is safe but produces the merge commit you explicitly wanted to avoid; 'always safer' ignores that rebasing private history is perfectly safe.
Correct — private, unpushed commits are yours alone to rewrite; rebase gives the clean linear result the golden rule permits.
variants.interviewTip: The trap is 'rebase = dangerous'. Reframe it as 'rebase = dangerous only on shared history' — for local, unpushed work it's the recommended way to stay current.

variants.question: `feat/search` is pushed to origin, but you are its only author and nobody has based work on it. After `git rebase main`, your `git push` is rejected as 'non-fast-forward'. Why, and what's the accepted move?
options: New hashes mean your line no longer descends from the remote tip; on a solo branch `--force-with-lease` publishes it
The rejection means the rebase corrupted the branch — reset back to `origin/feat/search` and redo all the work on top of it again
Run `git pull` first to merge the remote copy back in, since merging is always preferable to any form of force-pushing
Rebasing any pushed branch breaks the golden rule outright, so the one real fix is to undo the entire rebase completely
variants.rationale: Rebase replaced your commits with new-hash equivalents, so the remote tip is no longer an ancestor of your local tip — git correctly refuses a plain push. The golden rule targets history *others have built on*; a personal feature branch nobody consumes is fair game, and `--force-with-lease` publishes the rewrite while refusing to clobber the remote if someone pushed there in the meantime.
optionExplanations: Correct — rewritten hashes make the push non-fast-forward by design; `--force-with-lease` is the safety-checked way to update your own feature branch.
Nothing is corrupted — the rejection is git's expected response to rewritten history, not an error state to recover from.
Pulling would merge the pre-rebase and post-rebase lines, duplicating every commit — the classic self-inflicted zombie graph.
The golden rule is about commits others may have based work on; 'pushed' alone doesn't make history shared if you're the sole consumer.
variants.interviewTip: Name `--force-with-lease` unprompted and contrast it with bare `--force` — 'it aborts if the remote moved since my last fetch' shows you force-push with a seatbelt, not a hammer.

variants.question: An upstream maintainer rebased and force-pushed `release`. A teammate ran a default `git pull` on their local `release`, and `git log` now shows nearly every commit twice under different hashes. What produced the duplicates?
options: A network interruption mid-pull re-downloaded the same set of commits a second time
Force-push uploads a fresh copy of each commit right alongside the originals on the server
The teammate's reflog leaked into the branch history when the default pull replayed it back
The default pull merged the stale line with the rewritten one, and new hashes doubled each
variants.rationale: Rebase produces replacement commits with identical changes but new hashes. A default `git pull` is fetch + merge, so it stitched the teammate's stale line to the rewritten remote line — and since git identifies commits by hash, every original/replacement pair now coexists in the graph. Recovery is `git reset --hard origin/release` (after saving local work); prevention is never rewriting shared branches.
optionExplanations: Fetch is idempotent over content — objects are addressed by hash, so a retried download can never duplicate history.
Force-push moves the branch ref to the rewritten line; it doesn't store commits 'alongside' anything.
Reflogs are local, per-ref journals — they are never woven into a branch's commit history by a pull.
Correct — merge of the stale and rewritten lines plus hash-based identity equals every commit appearing twice.
variants.interviewTip: Walking through 'what does the teammate see after the force-push, and why does their pull make it worse?' is the strongest way to justify the golden rule — you're describing the blast radius, not reciting a slogan.

sections.heading: Unit testing with Vitest
paragraphs: A unit test isolates one piece of logic: arrange inputs, act, assert on the output. Vitest is the Vite-native runner — `describe` groups, `it` defines cases, `expect(result).toBe(expected)` asserts. Fast enough to run on every save.

Good tests assert observable behavior ('given an expired token, isValid returns false'), not implementation details ('it calls parseToken once'). Behavior-based tests survive refactors; implementation-based tests break when the code improves.

Determinism is what keeps a suite trusted: tests touching real time, randomness, or network are flaky by construction. Inject or mock those boundaries (`vi.useFakeTimers()`, `vi.mock(...)`) so the same input always yields the same result.
sections.summary: Test what your code does, not how it does it, and pin down time, randomness, and network so the same input always gives the same result.

variants.question: A test for 'trial expires after 14 days' calls the real `Date.now()` and started failing this week — the fixture data aged past the window. What's the durable fix?
options: Control time with fake timers or an injected clock to fix the date
Widen the assertion so it accepts either the expired or valid outcome
Delete the test, since the expiry logic here is really quite simple
Regenerate the fixture data on a set schedule every couple of weeks
variants.rationale: The test depends on wall-clock time — a hidden input that changes daily. Faking time (`vi.useFakeTimers()` + `vi.setSystemTime(...)`) or injecting a clock pins that input, so the test verifies the 14-day rule forever, not just for two weeks after someone refreshes fixtures.
optionExplanations: Correct — remove nondeterminism at the source; time becomes a controlled input.
A test that accepts both outcomes asserts nothing — it's a green light wired to stay green.
Simple logic with real dates is exactly where silent off-by-one expiry bugs live; the test earns its keep.
Scheduled human maintenance to keep a test green is a treadmill — and it *will* be forgotten.
variants.interviewTip: 'How do you deal with flaky tests?' — root-cause categories (time, randomness, network, shared state, order dependence) plus 'make the boundary injectable' is a complete, senior-sounding answer.

variants.question: A test asserts `describe('cart', () => { it('applies a random 5–15% loyalty discount', ...) })` by calling the real `Math.random()` and checking the total is within range. It passes ~99% of runs but fails intermittently in CI with no code change. What's the correct fix?
options: Add a retry so the test re-runs up to three times before it is marked failed
Mock randomness with `vi.spyOn(Math, 'random').mockReturnValue(0.5)` to fix it
Loosen the range check to accept 0–100% so the assertion can never fail at all
Run the test only on the local machine, never in CI, since CI boxes differ here
variants.rationale: The flake is nondeterminism from real randomness — a hidden input that varies each run, occasionally landing on a boundary the assertion mishandles. Stubbing `Math.random()` to a fixed value pins the input so the same computation runs every time, turning an intermittent test into a deterministic one that actually verifies the discount formula.
optionExplanations: Retries paper over flakiness — they hide a real nondeterminism bug and let genuinely broken code sneak through on a lucky re-run.
Correct — control the random boundary at the source; the discount becomes a fixed, deterministic input.
A 0–100% range asserts nothing about a 5–15% rule; it's a test wired to always pass.
'Skip it in CI' abandons the coverage exactly where it matters most and doesn't fix the nondeterminism.
variants.interviewTip: Retrying a flaky test is a smell, not a fix. Name the nondeterministic source — here, randomness — and pin it. Interviewers listen for whether you remove the cause or mask the symptom.

variants.question: A Vitest suite for a currency formatter calls the real `fetch('https://api.rates.example/latest')` to get exchange rates. It fails whenever the API is slow, rate-limits CI, or the rates drift from the asserted values. What's the durable fix?
options: Raise the test timeout to 30 seconds so slow API responses stop failing runs
Loosen the assertion to 'result is a non-empty string', as live rates vary
Schedule the suite to run overnight, when the rates API is under less load
Mock the network with `vi.mock` or a stubbed `fetch` so responses are fixed
variants.rationale: The test smuggles in three hidden inputs — latency, availability, and live data — none of which the formatter logic controls. Stubbing the fetch pins the response, so the unit test verifies formatting deterministically; whether the real API honors its contract is a separate, explicitly-marked integration concern, not something every unit run should gamble on.
optionExplanations: A longer timeout addresses one of three failure modes and makes the slow case slower — rate limits and drifting data still break the suite.
'Is a string' passes for garbage output — the assertion no longer verifies formatting at all.
Rescheduling dodges load but not outages or changing rates, and it decouples feedback from the push that caused a failure.
Correct — a stubbed response makes the network a controlled input; the unit test becomes deterministic and fast.
variants.interviewTip: Draw the line crisply: unit tests mock the network to test *your* logic; a thin, separate integration test checks the API contract. Conflating the two is how suites become slow and distrusted.

variants.question: `saveDraft` debounces calls by 300ms. Its test invokes it, then does `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 350))` before asserting the save fired once. It adds real wall-time to every run and still flakes on loaded CI machines. What's the right approach?
options: `vi.useFakeTimers()` then `vi.advanceTimersByTime(300)` to drive time and skip the race
Raise the real wait up to 1000ms so even a heavily loaded CI machine has ample slack here
Change the app's debounce down to 0ms so this test does not have to wait around at all now
Assert the save fired 'zero or one times' so scheduler jitter can never fail this test
variants.rationale: Sleeping real time makes the test both slow and probabilistic — 350ms is a bet that the event loop stays under 50ms of jitter, a bet loaded CI machines lose. Fake timers replace the clock with one the test owns: `advanceTimersByTime(300)` fires the debounce synchronously and exactly, so the test is instant and cannot race.
optionExplanations: Correct — time becomes a controlled input the test advances deliberately; no waiting, no race.
A bigger sleep shrinks the flake probability while growing the runtime — it's still a wager on machine load, just a slower one.
Rewriting production behavior to suit a test inverts the relationship — and a 0ms debounce is no longer a debounce.
'Zero or one' passes when the save never fires — the assertion is wired to stay green regardless of correctness.
variants.interviewTip: Real sleeps in unit tests fail twice: slow when they pass, flaky when the machine is busy. 'Fake timers make time an input I advance explicitly' is the one-line senior answer.

sections.heading: End-to-end testing with Playwright
paragraphs: Unit tests check parts; end-to-end tests check the assembled machine: Playwright drives a real browser through real flows — navigate, click, type, assert on what a user would see.

Prefer user-facing selectors — `getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })`, `getByLabel('Email')` — over CSS/XPath tied to DOM structure. They survive refactors and double as accessibility checks: if getByRole can't find your button, neither can a screen reader.

Playwright's assertions auto-wait and retry (`await expect(locator).toBeVisible()`) until the condition holds or a timeout expires, which eliminates the sleep-based flakiness older tools suffered — you synchronize on a real condition, not a guessed duration. The testing pyramid still applies: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, a thin crust of E2E on the critical paths.
sections.summary: Find elements the way a user would (by role and label) and wait on real conditions instead of guessing with sleeps.

variants.question: Why does Playwright's own documentation push `getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' })` over `page.locator('#app > div.form > button:nth-child(3)')`?
options: The `nth-child` pseudo-class is not supported inside `locator()` at all
Role selectors execute significantly faster inside the browser at runtime
Role/name selectors track what users perceive, so they survive refactors
Plain CSS selectors are now formally deprecated in modern Playwright APIs
variants.rationale: The structural selector encodes today's DOM shape — one wrapper div added and the test lies about the app being broken. The role selector encodes intent ('the button a user knows as Submit'), which changes only when the actual UX changes — and it fails if the button loses its accessible name, catching a11y regressions for free.
optionExplanations: nth-child works fine in locator() — which is part of the problem: it lets you write brittle tests.
Selector speed differences are negligible next to browser and network time.
Correct — resilience to refactors plus built-in accessibility pressure.
CSS selectors remain fully supported; the guidance is preference, not deprecation.
variants.interviewTip: 'How do you keep E2E suites from becoming flaky and hated?' — answer: user-facing selectors, auto-waiting assertions, test isolation, and keeping E2E thin per the pyramid. Four beats, well rehearsed.

variants.question: A test does `await page.waitForTimeout(3000)` then clicks a 'Checkout' button that appears after an async cart load. It passes locally but fails ~10% of the time in CI, where the machine is slower. What's the idiomatic Playwright fix?
options: Wrap the click in a try/catch and retry it inside a loop until it finally succeeds
Disable the test in CI entirely and run it only on the faster local developer machine
Bump the delay up to `waitForTimeout(8000)` to give the slower CI box far more headroom
Replace the sleep with auto-waiting `getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click()`
variants.rationale: A hardcoded `waitForTimeout` guesses at how long the async load takes — too short and it flakes on slow CI, too long and it wastes time. Playwright's locators and web-first assertions auto-wait and retry until the element is present and actionable, so the test synchronizes on the actual condition instead of a fragile fixed delay. That's the mechanism that kills sleep-based flakiness.
optionExplanations: A manual retry loop reinvents what Playwright's auto-waiting already does, worse and more verbosely.
Skipping in CI abandons coverage on the exact environment where the race actually surfaces.
A bigger fixed sleep just moves the flake threshold and slows every run; it still guesses instead of waiting on the real condition.
Correct — auto-waiting locators retry until the button is actually clickable, eliminating the timing guess entirely.
variants.interviewTip: Any `waitForTimeout` / `sleep` in an E2E test is a red flag. The senior answer: 'wait on a condition, not a duration' — Playwright's auto-waiting assertions do this for you.

variants.question: During a Tailwind migration a designer renames utility classes, and the E2E test using `page.locator('div.account-panel .btn-danger')` for the 'Close account' flow goes red — while the feature works perfectly in a real browser. What should replace the selector?
options: A longer XPath anchored on the panel's exact position in the DOM, being more precise than classes
`getByRole('button', { name: 'Close account' })` — targeting the user's view survives restyles
A `data-style` attribute mirroring the old class names so the existing selector keeps matching well
A pixel screenshot comparison of the button, since visual diffs can't break on a class rename
variants.rationale: The test just produced a false alarm: it failed while the product worked, because it encoded a styling detail users never see. A role + accessible-name locator encodes intent — 'the button a user knows as Close account' — so cosmetic refactors pass silently, and a failure now means something real: the control vanished or lost its accessible name, which is itself an a11y regression worth catching.
optionExplanations: Positional XPath is *more* brittle, not less — one wrapper div and it breaks again, still without telling you anything about the user experience.
Correct — selecting by role and name couples the test to user-perceived behavior instead of the styling layer.
Freezing dead class names into a shadow attribute preserves the coupling problem and adds maintenance debt to every future restyle.
Pixel diffs break on precisely this kind of change — restyled buttons render differently — and they can't click through a flow.
variants.interviewTip: Frame it as failure semantics: 'I want my E2E test to fail if and only if a user's experience broke.' Structural selectors fail on refactors; role/name selectors fail on real regressions.

variants.question: After clicking 'Apply coupon', a test immediately reads the price: `const text = await page.locator('.total').textContent(); expect(text).toBe('$36.00');`. It fails whenever the recalculation request is slow. Why, and what's the idiomatic fix?
options: `textContent()` is deprecated; using `innerText()` makes Playwright wait for network idle first here
Insert `await page.waitForTimeout(2000)` before the read so the slow request has time to fully finish
The one-shot read races the update; `expect(page.locator('.total')).toHaveText('$36.00')` retries
Wrap the `expect` inside a manual polling loop that re-reads the text every 100ms until it matches
variants.rationale: The moment you extract a value with `textContent()` and hand it to a plain `expect`, you've left Playwright's retry machinery — the assertion checks a stale snapshot taken before the recalculation landed. `expect(locator).toHaveText(...)` keeps the locator live: it re-reads the DOM on each retry until the condition holds, synchronizing on the actual outcome rather than a guess about timing.
optionExplanations: `textContent()` isn't deprecated and `innerText()` has no network-idle magic — the race is in the one-shot read, not the method name.
A fixed sleep trades one race for a slower one — still a duration-based guess that flakes when the request exceeds it.
Correct — web-first assertions operate on the locator, retrying the read itself until the expected state appears.
Hand-rolled polling reimplements `toHaveText` without its timeout handling, error reporting, or trace integration.
variants.interviewTip: The subtle trap is extracting a value and asserting on it — auto-waiting lives in `expect(locator)`, not `expect(value)`. Say 'keep assertions locator-based so they stay retryable' and you've flagged a mistake most juniors ship.

sections.heading: CI/CD: the pipeline as gatekeeper
paragraphs: Continuous Integration: every push triggers an automated pipeline — install, lint, type-check, test, build. The point is shrinking the distance between introducing a bug and hearing about it from weeks to minutes.

A typical GitHub Actions flow: on pull request, run the checks; merging is blocked until they're green plus a human review. Continuous Delivery/Deployment extends the green path: merged main auto-deploys to staging, then production — with prod gated manually (Delivery) or fully automatic (Deployment).

Pipelines fail-fast in order of cheapness: lint before tests, unit before E2E. And a red main is a stop-the-line event — the fix or the revert outranks new work, because everyone is building on top of it.
sections.summary: Run the cheapest checks first for fast feedback, and drop everything to fix a broken `main` since the whole team builds on it.

variants.question: A PR's pipeline runs: lint → unit tests → E2E tests → build. E2E is the slowest stage. Why do lint and unit tests run first?
options: Fail fast: cheap checks catch most failures in seconds, before E2E runs
E2E tests can only be run after a full deployment out to the production env now
Lint has to pass before the project's code will compile successfully at all
The pipeline simply runs its stages in plain alphabetical name order here
variants.rationale: Pipeline ordering is economics: fastest-and-most-likely-to-fail first. A typo that lint catches in 10 seconds shouldn't cost a full E2E run to discover. Same total coverage, radically better feedback latency for the common failure cases.
optionExplanations: Correct — fail-fast ordering optimizes time-to-feedback, which is the entire point of CI.
E2E runs against a preview or local server in CI — production deployment is not a prerequisite.
Linting is style/correctness analysis, independent of compilation; unlinted code compiles fine.
Stage order is authored deliberately in the workflow file; nothing is alphabetical.
variants.interviewTip: If asked to design a CI pipeline, narrate it in cost order — 'lint, type-check, unit, integration, E2E, build, deploy' — and mention branch protection on green checks. Structure is the signal.

variants.question: Your team's `main` branch pipeline goes red: a merged commit broke the build. A developer opens a fresh PR to add an unrelated new feature and asks to merge it 'since it's green on its own branch'. What does a healthy CI/CD culture do first?
options: Merge the new feature, since it's green on its own branch and unrelated to the break
Stop the line: fixing or reverting broken `main` outranks new work everyone builds on
Disable the failing check on `main` so the pipeline goes green and the work continues
Wait a full day to see whether the failure quietly resolves itself before acting at all
variants.rationale: A red `main` is a stop-the-line event. Everyone cuts new branches from `main` and merges back into it, so a broken `main` poisons every downstream branch and hides which failures are new. Restoring green — by fixing forward or reverting the offending commit — takes priority over any new feature, however clean that feature looks in isolation.
optionExplanations: Merging onto a broken `main` stacks new work atop the breakage and muddies which failures are the new PR's fault.
Correct — a red shared branch is stop-the-line; fix or revert before new work, because the whole team builds on `main`.
Silencing the check hides the breakage instead of resolving it — the bug ships and trust in the pipeline erodes.
Build failures don't self-heal; waiting just extends the window in which everyone inherits a broken base.
variants.interviewTip: 'Stop the line' is the phrase interviewers want. A red shared branch blocks the whole team, so its fix or revert always outranks new feature work — say that explicitly.

variants.question: A team inherited a pipeline that runs stages in this order: E2E suite (25 min) → build → unit tests → type-check → lint. Developers routinely wait half an hour to learn they missed a semicolon. What's the highest-leverage restructure?
options: Cache the E2E browser binaries so the 25-minute first stage begins a little bit sooner overall
Drop the lint and the type-check stages, since a passing E2E suite already proves the app works
Collapse everything into one single giant job so that at least all failures land in one report
Invert to cost order — lint, type-check, unit, build, E2E — so cheap checks report first
variants.rationale: The pipeline's coverage is fine; its *ordering* is economically backwards. Most failures are cheap ones — syntax, types, broken units — and this layout taxes every one of them with a 25-minute E2E toll before reporting. Reordering costs nothing, keeps identical total coverage, and collapses time-to-feedback for the common case from ~30 minutes to seconds.
optionExplanations: Shaving startup time off the wrong first stage still leaves a 20-plus-minute wait to hear about a lint error.
E2E proves happy paths render, not that types are sound or edge-case units behave — deleting cheap checks trades feedback for silence.
One mega-job still runs the slow work before reporting and gives up the clarity of per-stage failure signals.
Correct — fail-fast ordering: same checks, same rigor, radically faster feedback on the failures that happen most often.
variants.interviewTip: Pitch pipeline design as an economics problem: 'order stages by cost times likelihood of failure.' That one framing shows you optimize for time-to-feedback, which is the entire point of CI.

variants.question: One E2E test on `main` fails roughly one run in five. The team's habit is clicking 're-run jobs' until it goes green, and a dev proposes marking the whole E2E suite non-required 'since it's basically noise'. What does a healthy CI culture do instead?
options: Treat the flake as a defect: quarantine that one test under a ticket and keep the suite required
Accept the proposal, since non-required checks still show red for anyone who cares to inspect them
Configure the workflow to auto-retry every E2E job three times so people stop clicking the button
Move the E2E suite onto a nightly schedule where its flakiness can't block anyone's merge to `main`
variants.rationale: A CI gate is only worth what the team believes it means. 'Re-run until green' trains everyone to treat red as noise, which is exactly the state in which a real regression sails through on its second attempt. The fix is surgical: diagnose or quarantine the single flaky test under a tracked issue so the remaining suite stays trustworthy and required — preserving the gate instead of dismantling it.
optionExplanations: Correct — isolate the one bad test, keep the gate meaningful; flakiness is a bug in the test system and gets triaged like one.
Optional checks are ignored checks — within weeks the suite is decoration and its regressions ship unnoticed.
Automating the re-runs institutionalizes the coin flip: a genuine one-in-five failure now needs only one lucky retry to merge.
Nightly runs decouple failures from the commits that caused them, turning actionable PR feedback into next-morning archaeology.
variants.interviewTip: The phrase to land is 'trust in the pipeline is the asset'. Quarantine-with-a-ticket shows you can keep the gate strict without letting one bad test hold the whole team hostage.

sections.heading: The staging area and the three trees
paragraphs: Git juggles three versions of your project at once. The working directory is the files you edit on disk. The index (a.k.a. the staging area) is the snapshot you're assembling for the next commit. HEAD is the snapshot of your last commit — the tip of the current branch. `git status` is really a diff report between these three trees.

`git add` copies content from the working directory into the index; `git commit` writes the index into a new commit and moves HEAD to it. The index sitting *between* your edits and history is the whole point: it lets you compose a clean commit out of a messy working directory — stage two of five changed files, leave the rest for the next commit.

This is why `git diff` and `git diff --staged` show different things: the first compares working directory to index (what you haven't staged yet), the second compares index to HEAD (what you're about to commit). Reading both tells you exactly where every change currently lives.
sections.summary: Git tracks three snapshots — your edits, the staged index, and the last commit — and add/commit move content from one to the next.

variants.question: You edit `app.ts`, run `git add app.ts`, then edit `app.ts` again before committing. What does the commit contain?
options: Only the first edit — the version captured in the index by `git add`
Both edits combined, since git re-reads the file at the moment of commit
Nothing at all, because the second edit invalidated the earlier staging
Whichever edit is larger, as git keeps the more substantial staged copy
variants.rationale: `git add` snapshots the file's content into the index at that instant — it is not a live link to the file. The later edit lives only in the working directory, so the commit writes exactly what was staged: the first edit. `git status` will show `app.ts` as both staged and modified, which is git telling you the two trees now disagree.
optionExplanations: Correct — the index holds the content as of `git add`; the commit writes that snapshot, not the later edit.
Commit writes the index as it stands; it does not re-read the working directory for unstaged changes.
A second edit doesn't clear the index — the earlier staged content is still committed.
Git has no 'larger wins' rule; it commits the staged snapshot regardless of size.
variants.interviewTip: 'git add snapshots content, not a reference to the file' explains the classic 'staged and modified at once' status line — a detail that shows you understand the index as a real tree, not a checklist.

variants.question: You want to see only the changes you have NOT yet staged for the next commit. Which command shows exactly that?
options: `git diff --staged`, which prints every change queued for the commit
`git diff` with no arguments — working directory versus the index
`git log -p`, which walks the full patch history commit by commit
`git show HEAD`, which prints the contents of your most recent commit
variants.rationale: Bare `git diff` compares the working directory against the index, so it shows precisely what you've changed but not yet added. `git diff --staged` (or `--cached`) does the opposite comparison — index versus HEAD — showing what's already queued. Knowing which pair each command compares is what lets you stage deliberately instead of blindly `git add .`-ing everything.
optionExplanations: `--staged` compares index to HEAD — that's the already-staged changes, the opposite of what was asked.
Correct — plain `git diff` is working-directory-versus-index: exactly the unstaged changes.
`git log -p` shows historical commit patches, not the state of your current uncommitted work.
`git show HEAD` prints your last commit's diff, not anything about your working directory.
variants.interviewTip: Being able to say '`git diff` is working-vs-index, `git diff --staged` is index-vs-HEAD' signals you actually navigate the three trees rather than guessing at add/commit.

variants.question: After `git commit`, what happens to HEAD and the staging area?
options: HEAD stays put and the index is wiped clean of all its tracked content
HEAD rewinds one commit while the index keeps the newly committed files
Both HEAD and the index are reset to match the remote's current branch tip
HEAD moves to the new commit; the index now matches it, so both agree
variants.rationale: A commit writes the index into a new object and advances HEAD (via the current branch) to point at it. The index isn't emptied — it now equals the new HEAD, which is why `git status` reports 'nothing to commit' right after: index and HEAD are identical, and any remaining working-directory edits show up as unstaged. The three trees have simply re-aligned.
optionExplanations: The index isn't wiped — it comes to match the new commit; and HEAD does move forward.
Commit advances HEAD, it never rewinds it; that would be a reset.
Commit is local and touches nothing on the remote; the index is set from your staged content, not origin.
Correct — HEAD advances to the new commit and the index equals it, so status shows a clean tree.
variants.interviewTip: 'After a commit, index and HEAD are identical' is the mental model that makes `git reset`'s three modes (--soft/--mixed/--hard) click — each just decides which of the three trees to move.

variants.question: You've made five edits but want the next commit to include changes from only two files, saving the rest for later. What role does the staging area play?
options: It automatically groups related edits so git can split them into commits for you
It compresses the two chosen files, which is why staging is required before a commit
It lets you assemble a focused commit by adding only the two files you choose
It locks the other three files as read-only until the current commit completes
variants.rationale: The index exists precisely so a commit need not equal your entire working directory. You `git add` only the two files you want; the commit captures that curated snapshot while the other three stay modified-but-unstaged for a future commit. This is what makes atomic, single-purpose commits possible even when your working tree is a pile of half-finished work.
optionExplanations: Git doesn't infer 'related' edits or auto-split — *you* choose what to stage; the grouping is manual.
Staging isn't about compression; it's about selecting which changes the next commit captures.
Correct — staging lets you hand-pick the two files so the commit is focused, leaving the rest for later.
Staging never locks files; the unstaged three remain freely editable in the working directory.
variants.interviewTip: Frame the index as 'the commit-composer': it's why you can keep a messy working tree yet still ship clean, atomic commits — a habit reviewers and `git bisect` both reward.

sections.heading: Undoing changes: reset, revert, restore
paragraphs: Three verbs, three jobs. `git restore` throws away uncommitted changes in the working directory or unstages files — it operates on your current mess, not on history. `git reset` moves the current branch pointer to another commit, optionally rewriting the index and working tree with `--soft`/`--mixed`/`--hard`. `git revert` creates a *new* commit that undoes a previous one, leaving history intact.

The dividing line is whether the work is shared. Reset rewrites history, so it's safe only on local, unpushed commits — the same golden rule that governs rebase. Revert adds forward history instead of erasing it, so it's the correct tool for undoing something already pushed to a branch others use: nobody's clone diverges because nothing was rewritten.

`reset` modes differ by how many trees they touch: `--soft` moves only the branch pointer (your changes land back in the index), `--mixed` (the default) also resets the index (changes return to the working directory), and `--hard` resets the working directory too — discarding those changes, which is the one genuinely destructive mode.
sections.summary: Restore fixes uncommitted files, reset rewrites local history, and revert safely undoes a pushed commit by adding a new one.

variants.question: A bad commit was pushed to shared `main` an hour ago and several teammates have already pulled it. What's the correct way to undo it?
options: `git reset --hard HEAD~1` locally, then force-push the rewound `main`
`git revert`, which adds a new commit that cancels out the bad one
`git restore .`, discarding the bad commit's files across the tree
`git reset --soft HEAD~1`, quietly dropping the commit from history
variants.rationale: `main` is shared and the commit is already in teammates' clones — rewriting history now would force-push over commits others hold, diverging everyone. `git revert` instead records a new commit that applies the inverse change, so history only moves forward and every clone fast-forwards cleanly. Revert is the shared-branch undo; reset is for local, unpushed work.
optionExplanations: Reset + force-push rewrites shared history — the exact golden-rule violation that leaves every teammate's `main` diverged.
Correct — revert adds an inverse commit, undoing the change without rewriting anything others already have.
`git restore` only touches uncommitted working-tree files; it can't undo a commit that's already in history.
`--soft` still rewrites the branch pointer, so publishing it demands a force-push — unsafe on shared `main`.
variants.interviewTip: 'Revert for shared history, reset for local history' is the crisp pairing. Add 'revert moves history forward, it never erases it' and you've explained *why* it's the safe choice.

variants.question: You just ran `git reset --soft HEAD~1`. What state are you in?
options: The last commit is undone, but its changes are staged in the index, ready to re-commit
The last commit and every change it made are permanently gone from the repository
Nothing changed yet — `--soft` only previews the reset until you confirm it explicitly
The working directory is wiped back to match the commit before the one you removed
variants.rationale: `--soft` moves only the branch pointer back one commit and touches neither the index nor the working directory. The result: the commit is 'undone' as history, but everything it contained is sitting staged in the index, ready to be re-committed — which is exactly how you amend or split a commit. It's the least destructive reset mode.
optionExplanations: Correct — `--soft` rewinds only the pointer; the commit's content stays staged in the index.
`--soft` discards nothing; the changes survive in the index. Only `--hard` would touch the working tree.
Reset isn't a preview or dry-run — it acts immediately; `--soft` just limits *what* it moves.
Wiping the working directory is `--hard` behavior; `--soft` leaves working files completely untouched.
variants.interviewTip: The clean summary: `--soft` moves the pointer, `--mixed` also resets the index, `--hard` also resets the working tree. Reciting which trees each mode touches is the answer interviewers want.

variants.question: You edited a config file, saved it, but haven't staged or committed — and now you want the file back exactly as the last commit had it. Which command does that?
options: `git revert HEAD`, since it reverses the change made to the config file
`git reset --hard HEAD~1`, moving the branch back before the config edit
`git restore config.ts`, discarding the unstaged edits to that one file
`git commit --amend`, folding the reverted config back into the last commit
variants.rationale: The edit is uncommitted, living only in the working directory, so this is a job for `git restore` — it overwrites the named file with the version from the index (or HEAD), throwing the local change away. Reset and revert both operate on committed history and are the wrong altitude for discarding a single uncommitted file.
optionExplanations: `revert` undoes a *commit*; there's no commit here to reverse — the edit is still uncommitted.
`reset --hard HEAD~1` rewinds a whole commit and nukes more than the one file — wrong scope and destructive.
Correct — `git restore <file>` discards the uncommitted edit, restoring that file from the last commit.
`--amend` rewrites the previous commit; it does nothing to discard an unstaged working-directory edit.
variants.interviewTip: Modern git split the overloaded `git checkout` into `git restore` (files) and `git switch` (branches). Naming `restore` for discarding uncommitted file changes signals you know the current, less foot-gun-prone commands.

variants.question: What is the fundamental difference between `git reset` and `git revert` when undoing a commit?
options: `reset` only works on merge commits, whereas `revert` works on any ordinary commit
`reset` moves the branch pointer to rewrite history; `revert` adds a new inverse commit
`revert` deletes the target commit from history; `reset` merely hides it from the log view
They are aliases with identical effects; `revert` is simply the newer preferred spelling
variants.rationale: `reset` relocates the branch pointer, so commits after the target fall out of the branch's history — it rewrites, which is safe only locally. `revert` leaves all history in place and appends a new commit whose diff is the inverse of the target, so the undo is itself recorded. That's why revert is the shared-branch tool and reset is the local one.
optionExplanations: Neither is restricted to merge commits; both operate on ordinary commits (reverting a merge just needs `-m`).
Correct — reset rewrites history by moving the pointer; revert preserves history by adding an inverse commit.
It's backwards: `revert` *keeps* the commit and adds an inverse; `reset` is the one that drops commits from the branch.
They are not aliases — one rewrites history and one appends to it, with opposite safety profiles on shared branches.
variants.interviewTip: 'Reset rewrites, revert appends' is the one-liner. Tie it to sharedness — 'so I revert anything pushed and reset only local work' — to show the safety reasoning behind the choice.

sections.heading: Remotes and tracking branches
paragraphs: A remote (`origin`, by convention) is a named URL for another copy of the repo. Your clone keeps remote-tracking branches like `origin/main` — read-only local bookmarks recording where the remote's branches were *as of your last sync*. They don't update live; they move only when you fetch.

`git fetch` downloads new commits and updates those `origin/*` bookmarks, changing nothing in your working branches — pure, safe information. `git pull` is `fetch` plus an immediate `merge` (or `rebase`) of the tracking branch into your current branch. `git push` uploads your commits and moves the remote's branch pointer to match yours, if it can fast-forward.

An 'upstream' link binds your local branch to a remote-tracking branch, which is how bare `git push`/`git pull` know where to go and how `git status` can say 'ahead 2, behind 1'. That ahead/behind count is computed by comparing your branch to its cached `origin/*` bookmark — so it's only as fresh as your last fetch.
sections.summary: Fetch just updates your read-only origin/* bookmarks; pull fetches then merges; push uploads and fast-forwards the remote.

variants.question: What is the practical difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
options: `fetch` downloads commits but changes no working branch; `pull` fetches then merges
`fetch` retrieves only branch names as labels; `pull` retrieves the actual commit data
`fetch` works over SSH exclusively, whereas `pull` is the HTTPS equivalent command
`fetch` uploads your local commits to origin; `pull` downloads the remote's commits
variants.rationale: `fetch` is the safe half: it downloads new objects and advances your `origin/*` bookmarks, but your checked-out branch and working directory are untouched. `pull` chains a `merge` (or `rebase`) onto that fetch, immediately integrating the remote work into your current branch. Knowing pull = fetch + merge is what lets you fetch first, inspect, then integrate deliberately.
optionExplanations: Correct — fetch updates tracking branches only; pull fetches and then merges into your current branch.
Fetch downloads real commit objects, not just names — it's a full content sync of the tracking refs.
Both work over any transport; the protocol has nothing to do with fetch-versus-pull semantics.
That reverses push and pull — fetch and pull both *download*; neither uploads your commits.
variants.interviewTip: 'pull = fetch + merge' is the sentence to have ready. Add that you often 'fetch, review with `git log origin/main`, then merge' to show you integrate deliberately rather than blindly pulling.

variants.question: Your `git status` says 'Your branch is behind origin/main by 3 commits'. You know for a fact a teammate pushed 5 commits an hour ago. Why the mismatch?
options: The remote silently rejected 2 of the teammate's 5 pushed commits as duplicates
`origin/main` is a cached bookmark reflecting your last fetch, not the live remote
`git status` always undercounts by two to leave a safety margin against races
Your branch has quietly diverged, so status can no longer count commits accurately
variants.rationale: The 'ahead/behind' numbers compare your branch to the local `origin/main` bookmark, which only advances when you fetch. If your last fetch predated 2 of the 5 pushes, your cached bookmark is stale and status reports what it knows — 3, not 5. A `git fetch` updates the bookmark and the count corrects itself. Tracking branches are snapshots, not live queries.
optionExplanations: Nothing was rejected; the remote has all 5. Your local *view* of it is simply out of date.
Correct — status compares against the cached `origin/main`, which only updates on fetch, so it lags the live remote.
Status reports the true count against your tracking ref; there is no built-in 'safety margin' fudge.
Being behind isn't divergence — divergence means both sides have unique commits; here you've simply not fetched the latest.
variants.interviewTip: 'origin/main is a snapshot from my last fetch, not a live view' is a subtle point that separates people who understand git's offline model from those who think of it like a live server query.

variants.question: You want to see what a teammate pushed to `main` WITHOUT touching your own in-progress branch or merging anything. Which command is exactly right?
options: `git pull origin main`, then just discard the merge if you don't like the changes
`git push origin main`, which syncs your view with the remote's latest commits
`git merge origin/main` to preview the incoming commits before deciding to keep them
`git fetch`, then inspect the updated `origin/main` with `git log`
variants.rationale: `fetch` is the read-only sync: it advances your `origin/*` bookmarks without altering your current branch or working tree, so you can then `git log origin/main` or diff against it to review the incoming work in total safety. Pull would merge immediately, push would try to upload, and a bare merge would integrate the commits — all of which change your branch, which is exactly what you wanted to avoid.
optionExplanations: Pull merges into your branch on the spot — 'discard it after' means untangling a merge you didn't need to make.
Push uploads *your* commits; it does nothing to show you a teammate's incoming work.
`merge origin/main` integrates those commits into your branch — that's the opposite of leaving it untouched.
Correct — fetch updates the bookmarks read-only; `git log origin/main` then shows the incoming commits safely.
variants.interviewTip: 'Fetch is always safe' is worth stating outright — it never changes your working branch, so it's the right first move whenever you want to look before you leap.

variants.question: You create a brand-new local branch and run `git push`, which errors with 'no upstream branch'. What does setting an upstream with `git push -u origin feature` accomplish?
options: It force-pushes past the error by overwriting whatever origin currently holds
It links your branch to `origin/feature`, so bare `push`/`pull` know the target
It converts your local branch into a protected branch that cannot be deleted
It merges `origin/main` into your feature branch to resolve the missing upstream
variants.rationale: A new local branch has no upstream, so git doesn't know where a bare `git push` should send it. `-u` (`--set-upstream`) records the association between your branch and `origin/feature`; from then on plain `git push` and `git pull` resolve automatically, and `git status` can report ahead/behind against that tracking branch. It's a one-time bit of wiring, not a force or a merge.
optionExplanations: `-u` sets tracking; it has nothing to do with force-pushing or overwriting remote content.
Correct — `-u` binds the branch to `origin/feature`, so future bare push/pull and ahead/behind counts just work.
Branch protection is a server-side (e.g. GitHub) setting, entirely unrelated to the upstream link.
Setting upstream performs no merge; it only records where this branch pushes and pulls.
variants.interviewTip: Explaining that `-u` wires the upstream so 'bare push/pull and the ahead/behind counter all resolve automatically afterward' shows you understand tracking branches, not just the command you paste after the error.

sections.heading: Resolving merge conflicts
paragraphs: A conflict happens when two branches changed the same lines of the same file in incompatible ways — git can combine non-overlapping edits automatically, but overlapping ones it refuses to guess about. It pauses the merge and marks the file with `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>` fences: your side above the divider, theirs below.

Resolving means editing the file into the correct final state — which is often neither side verbatim but a hand-merged combination — then removing the conflict markers, `git add`-ing the file to mark it resolved, and running `git commit` (or `git merge --continue`) to seal the merge. `git status` lists exactly which files still need resolution.

Conflicts are a normal signal, not an error to fear: they mean two people evolved the same code and a human must decide intent. You reduce them by merging/rebasing from the main line often (small, frequent integrations conflict less than one giant merge) and by keeping changes narrowly scoped. `git merge --abort` always backs you out to the pre-merge state if you'd rather retreat and try again.
sections.summary: A conflict is git asking a human to reconcile overlapping edits — resolve the file, remove the markers, then add and commit.

variants.question: Git pauses a merge reporting a conflict in `utils.ts`. What has actually happened?
options: The repository is now corrupted and must be re-cloned from origin to recover
Both branches edited overlapping lines, so git needs a human to reconcile them
Your local copy of `utils.ts` was deleted and git halted to avoid losing more
A network timeout interrupted the merge partway through and left it incomplete
variants.rationale: A conflict is git being honest, not broken: both branches changed the same region of `utils.ts` in ways it can't safely auto-combine, so it stops and hands you the decision. It marks the competing versions inside the file and waits. Nothing is corrupt or lost — the merge is simply paused until a human encodes the correct intent.
optionExplanations: Nothing is corrupted — a conflict is a normal, recoverable pause, and `--abort` cleanly restores the pre-merge state.
Correct — overlapping edits to the same lines can't be auto-merged, so git asks a human to reconcile.
The file isn't deleted; it's present with conflict markers showing both competing versions.
Merges are local and don't time out over the network; the pause is intentional, not an interruption.
variants.interviewTip: Reframing conflicts as 'git asking a human to decide intent' rather than 'an error' signals maturity — juniors panic at conflicts, seniors treat them as routine and resolve them calmly.

variants.question: After editing a conflicted file down to the final correct code and deleting the `<<<`/`===`/`>>>` markers, what must you do to complete the merge?
options: `git add` the file to mark it resolved, then commit to finish the merge
Nothing further — saving the cleaned-up file auto-completes the paused merge
Run `git merge --abort`, which now finalizes the resolution you just wrote
Force-push the branch immediately so origin records the resolved version first
variants.rationale: Editing the file fixes the content, but git still sees it as 'unmerged' until you `git add` it — that's the signal that you've resolved this path. Once every conflicted file is staged, `git commit` (or `git merge --continue`) writes the merge commit and the merge is done. Saving alone doesn't tell git you're finished; the `add` is the explicit 'resolved' marker.
optionExplanations: Correct — `git add` marks the file resolved, then a commit seals the merge.
Saving doesn't clear the unmerged state — git still needs the `git add` to know you resolved it.
`--abort` throws your resolution away and rewinds to the pre-merge state — the opposite of finishing.
Nothing needs pushing to finish a merge; the merge commit is created locally by `add` + `commit`.
variants.interviewTip: The step people forget is that `git add` *is* the 'mark resolved' action. Saying 'edit, remove markers, add to mark resolved, commit' in that order shows you've actually driven a merge to completion.

variants.question: Halfway through resolving a big, messy merge you decide you'd rather back out entirely and take a different approach. What returns you to the exact state from before the merge began?
options: `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, which rewinds one commit past the merge you started
`git commit` with an empty message, which cancels the in-progress merge cleanly
`git checkout .`, discarding the conflict markers to end the merge attempt
`git merge --abort`, which unwinds the merge and restores the pre-merge state
variants.rationale: `git merge --abort` is purpose-built for exactly this: it discards the in-progress merge, including all conflict markers and partial resolutions, and restores your branch and working tree to precisely where they were before you ran `git merge`. The other options either act on commits that don't exist yet (the merge isn't committed) or only touch files without unwinding the merge state.
optionExplanations: There's no merge commit yet to rewind — the merge is still in progress, so `HEAD~1` targets the wrong thing.
Committing would *finish* the merge with a broken state, not cancel it; empty-message commits are also rejected by default.
`checkout .` only overwrites working files; it leaves git still mid-merge with the merge state intact.
Correct — `git merge --abort` cleanly unwinds the merge and restores the exact pre-merge state.
variants.interviewTip: Knowing `git merge --abort` (and its cousin `git rebase --abort`) exists is a confidence signal: you can start a risky integration knowing there's always a clean, single-command retreat.

variants.question: Your team keeps hitting large, painful merge conflicts when long-lived feature branches finally merge. What's the most effective way to reduce them?
options: Assign one person to own every merge so conflicts are handled consistently
Always pick 'accept theirs' on conflicts to resolve them in a fraction of the time
Integrate from the main line often, in small increments, instead of one giant merge
Switch the whole team from merge to rebase, which is incapable of producing conflicts
variants.rationale: Conflict size scales with how far two branches have drifted apart. A branch that merges or rebases from `main` daily reconciles a little at a time, so overlaps are tiny and rare; a branch that hides for three weeks reconciles all that divergence at once. Small, frequent integration is the structural fix — it attacks the cause (drift) rather than the symptom (the eventual painful merge).
optionExplanations: A dedicated merger doesn't shrink the divergence — the giant conflict still exists, just always dumped on one person.
'Always accept theirs' silently discards your side's work; it's data loss dressed up as a resolution strategy.
Correct — frequent small integrations keep branches close to `main`, so conflicts stay tiny and infrequent.
Rebase still produces conflicts on overlapping edits — it replays commits, and each replay can conflict just like a merge.
variants.interviewTip: 'Conflicts scale with divergence, so integrate early and often' is the systemic answer. It shows you prevent conflicts through workflow rather than just grinding through them after the fact.

sections.heading: Test coverage and the test pyramid
paragraphs: The test pyramid describes a healthy suite's *shape*: a broad base of fast, isolated unit tests, a smaller middle band of integration tests that check components working together, and a thin top of end-to-end tests over the critical user journeys. The shape follows from cost — unit tests are cheap and stable, E2E tests are slow and flakier, so you want many of the former and few of the latter.

Coverage measures which lines/branches your tests execute, expressed as a percentage. It's a useful *floor detector* — 20% coverage tells you most code is untested — but a treacherous *target*: 100% coverage can still miss every bug if the tests assert nothing meaningful. Coverage tells you what was *run*, never whether the right things were *checked*.

The classic anti-pattern is the 'ice-cream cone' — a fat layer of slow E2E tests propping up a suite with few units — which is slow, flaky, and expensive to maintain. Chasing a coverage number also warps behavior: teams write trivial getter tests to hit a quota while real edge cases go unexercised. Aim for confidence on the paths that matter, not a round number on a dashboard.
sections.summary: Favor many fast unit tests over few slow E2E ones, and treat coverage as a floor to notice gaps, never a target to hit.

variants.question: A module reports 100% line coverage. Why might it still be effectively untested?
options: Coverage above 90% disables the assertion engine, so nothing is actually verified
Line coverage only counts comments, not the executable statements around them
The tests run every line but may assert nothing meaningful about the results
100% coverage forces every test into a single file, hiding most real failures
variants.rationale: Coverage records which lines *executed* during the test run — not whether any assertion checked their output. A test that calls a function through all its branches but never asserts on the result paints the code green while verifying nothing. That's why coverage is a floor detector (low means gaps) but a poor target (high can be hollow).
optionExplanations: There's no such mechanism — assertions run independently of the coverage percentage.
Line coverage measures executable lines, not comments; comments are ignored entirely.
Correct — coverage proves a line ran, not that any assertion meaningfully checked its behavior.
Coverage percentage has no bearing on file layout; tests can live anywhere regardless of the number.
variants.interviewTip: 'Coverage tells you what ran, not what was checked' is the line to land. It shows you value assertion quality over a vanity metric — a distinction that separates thoughtful testers from quota-chasers.

variants.question: A suite is 80% end-to-end tests and 20% unit tests, runs for 40 minutes, and flakes constantly. What shape is this, and what's the fix?
options: It's an ice-cream cone; push logic down into fast unit tests and keep E2E thin
It's a textbook pyramid already; the slowness is just an unavoidable cost of testing
It's a balanced diamond shape, so the only real fix available is faster CI hardware
It's under-tested overall; the fix is simply adding many more end-to-end tests on top
variants.rationale: An E2E-heavy, unit-light suite is the inverted pyramid — the 'ice-cream cone' — and it's slow and flaky precisely because it leans on the most expensive, least stable layer. The fix is to move most verification down into fast, deterministic unit tests and keep only a thin E2E crust over the critical journeys, restoring the pyramid's cost-efficient shape.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is the ice-cream cone; rebalance by driving logic into unit tests and keeping E2E thin.
A pyramid is unit-*heavy*; this is the inverse, and the slowness is a symptom of that bad shape, not inherent.
It's not a diamond — it's top-heavy; throwing hardware at it treats the symptom, not the inverted shape.
Adding more E2E makes the cone worse — slower and flakier; the missing layer is fast unit tests.
variants.interviewTip: Name the 'ice-cream cone' by name and prescribe 'push logic down to unit tests, keep E2E thin.' The vocabulary plus the fix shows you diagnose suite shape, not just individual tests.

variants.question: Management mandates '90% coverage or the build fails'. Within a sprint, coverage hits 90% but bugs still ship. What most likely happened?
options: The coverage tool miscounted, so the real figure never actually reached the 90% goal
Developers wrote trivial, assertion-light tests to hit the quota, not test behavior
90% is simply too low a bar; only a strict 100% mandate reliably prevents shipping bugs
Coverage and bug rate are unrelated, so no test strategy could have changed this outcome
variants.rationale: A coverage *target* becomes a metric to game: the fastest way to 90% is trivial tests that execute code without meaningfully asserting on it, inflating the number while real edge cases stay unchecked. The lines ran, so coverage rose; nothing was verified, so bugs shipped. This is why coverage works as a floor ('too low = gaps') but corrodes into theater when set as a goal.
optionExplanations: Gaming the metric, not miscounting, is the usual cause — the tools count executed lines accurately.
Correct — a coverage quota incentivizes trivial tests that raise the number without verifying behavior.
Raising the target to 100% intensifies the gaming; the problem is targeting coverage at all, not the threshold.
They're correlated when tests assert well — the failure here is hollow tests, not an absence of any link.
variants.interviewTip: Cite Goodhart's law in spirit: 'when coverage becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.' Proposing coverage as a *floor with review of assertion quality* shows you'd design the incentive correctly.

variants.question: Why does the test pyramid recommend MANY unit tests but only a FEW end-to-end tests?
options: End-to-end tests are banned from CI environments, so their count must be kept minimal
Unit tests can only ever check one single line, so a great many are always required
Unit tests are fast and stable while E2E tests are slow and flaky, so cost sets the ratio
The two kinds test entirely different code, and units happen to cover far more of it
variants.rationale: The pyramid is an economics diagram. Unit tests are cheap to write, run in milliseconds, and rarely flake, so you can afford thousands. E2E tests spin up a real browser and full stack — slow and more prone to timing flakiness — so each one costs far more per unit of confidence. You get the best confidence-per-second by concentrating coverage in the cheap layer and reserving E2E for a few critical journeys.
optionExplanations: E2E tests run in CI routinely; they're kept few for cost and stability reasons, not because they're forbidden.
A unit test can cover a whole function or module, not a single line — the count is about cost, not granularity.
Correct — the ratio follows cost: unit tests are fast and stable, E2E slow and flakier, so many-vs-few is optimal.
They overlap heavily — E2E exercises the same logic end-to-end; the ratio is about cost per test, not disjoint code.
variants.interviewTip: Frame the pyramid as 'confidence per second': cheap, stable units at the base, expensive, flaky E2E at the tip. Leading with the cost reasoning beats reciting the shape from memory.
